claims.text: A hybrid model that explicitly includes defect- and oxygen-induced scattering will substantially improve predictions of temperature-dependent electrical conductivity for bulk HfNbTaTiZr containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
Conventional analytical conductivity models for this alloy assume a perfect, defect-free crystal.
The target material is an as-cast bulk HfNbTaTiZr alloy containing 1 wt.% oxygen.
The oxygen in the target material occurs as interstitial oxygen and/or at grain boundaries.
The hybrid framework combines DFT calculations with effective-medium and defect-scattering models.
Including oxygen interstitials and microstructural imperfections will appropriately adjust electronic-structure predictions and carrier-scattering rates.
Controlled experimental conductivity data are available for 1 wt.% oxygen specimens over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Oxygen-related defect states alter the electronic density of states in HfNbTaTiZr.
Grain boundaries and dislocations alter carrier-scattering rates in the target alloy.
Explicit treatment of defect-induced electron scattering and impurity states will reduce the discrepancy between ideal-crystal predictions and measured conductivity.
Oxygen and microstructural defects modify high-temperature carrier dynamics.
The hybrid model will predict conductivity within ±20% of experiment in both specified temperature regimes.
The hybrid model will outperform standard defect-free analytical predictions.
Existing analytical predictions often exceed 30% error against measured conductivity over the target temperature ranges.
The approach is applicable only to bulk HfNbTaTiZr with approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
The approach is valid only over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The anticipated reduction from greater than 30% error to within ±20% is based on analogous multiscale studies in related complex alloys.
